Usage guidance

Types

Buttons come in two functional types — the choice is about whether the button maintains state, not about prominence.

Standard button — Fires a single action and returns to rest. Use for submit, save, delete, and open.

Toggle button — Fires an action and maintains a selected or unselected state. Use where an action needs to stay active, like toggling a view mode or a formatting option in a toolbar.

Don't use disabled to represent a toggled-off state. Disabled means the component is unavailable. For an inactive toggle, use the unselected state of a toggle button.

Behavior

A button triggers a single, discrete action — submit, save, delete, open. Use it as the primary call to action on a surface, and pair it with the toggle type in toolbars and command bars where on/off behavior is needed.

By default, a button fires once and returns to rest. Specify the toggle type when you need the button to keep its state across activations — and when you do, communicate the selected state with the toggle’s icon and label treatments rather than swapping to a disabled appearance.

When you place an icon on a toggle button, swap between Regular and Filled glyphs as the state changes — Regular when unselected, Filled when selected.

Toggle buttons need to hold their width across selection. The label weight changes from regular to semibold when selected, and that shift would otherwise resize the container. Reserve the layout space at the semibold width up front (ghost element). Standard (non-toggle) buttons don’t need this.

Layout

Use only one Primary button per surface. Multiple Primaries flatten the hierarchy and create visual noise — pick the single loudest action and demote the rest to Secondary, Outline, or Subtle.

The Icon and text layout is the default — the label improves discoverability. Reach for Icon only when space is tight and the icon is unambiguous on its own. Icon only changes the form factor (circular, no label) and needs both an aria-label and a visible alternative — typically a tooltip.

Don’t mix icon sizes across button sizes. Small buttons use 16px icons; Medium and Large use 20px. Always apply the correct radius token per layout — atomic-small, atomic-medium, or atomic-large for Icon and text by size, and atomic-circular for Icon only.

Accessibility

Icon only buttons need a paired affordance. The aria-label describes the action for screen readers; a visible alternative — usually a tooltip — supports sighted people who don’t recognize the icon. State both; neither is optional.

When the toggle type is in use, set aria-pressed to reflect the current state so assistive technology can announce the toggle.

When prefers-reduced-motion: reduce is set, all button transitions should be instant. Buttons don’t use scale, translate, or opacity animation; color-only transitions are acceptable under reduced motion.

Content

Use functional typography on button labels. Buttons are interactive UI chrome, not editorial content — don’t apply content-set type like Segoe Serif or other editorial styles to a button label.
